claims.claim: Binga Bank opened in 1908 as a private bank, the first Black-owned bank in the Northern United States.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on the opening year; some popular accounts say Binga arrived in Chicago in 1893 vs. 1892 — a biographical detail that does not affect the bank claim.
claims.evidence: Kansas City Fed history book (Todd, 2019) describes Binga's private bank opening in 1908 and identifies it as the first Black-owned bank in the Northern U.S.
claims.notes: 'First in the Northern U.S.' is a regional distinction, not a national first — do not present it as the first Black bank in America.
claims.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, Let Us Put Our Money Together: The Founding of America's First Black Banks (2019), https://www.kansascityfed.org/AboutUs/documents/5640/Let-Us-Put-Our-Money-Together-book-FINAL-2019.pdf

claims.claim: Binga Bank received a state charter in 1921 as Binga State Bank; it closed in 1930 during the Great Depression.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on charter year or closure year.
claims.evidence: Kansas City Fed (2019); BlackPast entry; Hayner biography all agree on the 1921 state charter and the 1930 closure.
claims.notes: Causes of the 1930 closure are not established from primary evidence in this session — do not attribute it to a single cause.
claims.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (2019); BlackPast.org, 'Jesse Binga (1865-1950)'

claims.claim: At its 1921 state-bank opening, Binga State Bank held deposits of more than $200,000; within three years deposits exceeded $1.3 million.
claims.contradictory_evidence: No competing figures located; BlackPast and Hayner-excerpt accounts agree, but both are secondary and no examiner or call-report records were consulted.
claims.evidence: BlackPast reports the $200,000 opening figure and $1.3 million within three years; Don Hayner biography excerpt corroborates the growth narrative.
claims.notes: These figures illustrate savings mobilization. They should be labeled as reported figures, not verified balance-sheet data.
claims.source: BlackPast.org; Don Hayner biography excerpt (Northwestern University Press)

claims.claim: Binga Bank operated from premises at 3633 S. State Street, Chicago.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Other secondary accounts mention State Street near 35th/36th Place, suggesting the bank occupied more than one premises over its life.
claims.evidence: National Park Service, Black Metropolis Historic District National Register nomination (1985), identifies 3633 S. State Street as Binga Bank.
claims.notes: Only the 3633 S. State Street location is verified via a federal document; the full address chronology across 1908-1930 is UNRESOLVED.
claims.source: National Park Service, Black Metropolis Historic District nomination (1985), https://npgallery.nps.gov/NRHP/GetAsset/NRHP/64000173_text

claims.claim: In 1933 Jesse Binga was convicted of embezzling $22,000 from the bank and sentenced to ten years; he was released after three years following petitions and later pardoned (1941).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Popular accounts sometimes frame the prosecution as racially motivated; no primary court or parole records were consulted to confirm details.
claims.evidence: BlackPast reports the 1933 conviction, $22,000 figure, ten-year sentence, release after three years, and pardon.
claims.notes: Do not present the 'selective prosecution' narrative as fact without primary evidence; the conviction facts themselves rest on a single secondary source.
claims.source: BlackPast.org, 'Jesse Binga (1865-1950)'

claims.claim: Binga's bank converted Black household savings into formal banking capital: Black Chicagoans deposited savings there, and children used Binga-branded tin banks.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; the claim is anecdotal and secondary.
claims.evidence: Don Hayner biography excerpt describes savings deposits, Binga-branded tin banks for children, and a Black homebuyer seeking a loan from Binga.
claims.notes: Useful illustration of the savings-mobilization role, but anecdotal — keep it clearly sourced to Hayner.
claims.source: Don Hayner, Binga: The Rise and Fall of Chicago's First Black Banker (Northwestern University Press), via biography excerpt

claims.claim: Binga Bank provided rare white-collar employment for Black Chicagoans.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; no employment rosters or headcounts were found.
claims.evidence: BlackPast reports the bank employed Black workers in white-collar positions rare for the era.
claims.notes: The direction of the claim (employment role) is supported by the bank's existence and clientele; the scale is unknown.
claims.source: BlackPast.org

claims.claim: Douglass National Bank was founded by Anthony Overton and operated from the Overton Hygienic Building at 3619-3627 S. State Street; it failed in 1932.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Founding year is given as 1922 (Kansas City Fed) in some sources and 1923 in others.
claims.evidence: Library of Congress guide (citing Weems 2020) identifies Overton's bank; NPS Black Metropolis nomination gives the Hygienic Building address; Kansas City Fed gives the 1922 opening; multiple sources agree on the 1932 failure.
claims.notes: The founding year dispute (1922 vs. 1923) is the only unresolved detail; it should be flagged in the timeline.
claims.source: Library of Congress, African Americans in Business guide; National Park Service; Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (2019)

claims.claim: Douglass National Bank was the second nationally chartered Black-owned bank in the United States (after the First National Bank of Boley, Oklahoma).
claims.contradictory_evidence: An NPS page about the Overton Hygienic Building describes it as the 'first nationally chartered African American-owned bank' — this contradicts LoC/Weems and Kansas City Fed.
claims.evidence: Library of Congress guide, citing Robert E. Weems Jr. (2020), identifies it as the second; Kansas City Fed (2019) concurs. The NPS phrasing appears to be an error or a Chicago-framed shorthand.
claims.notes: This contradiction must be visible in the brief; use 'second' per the stronger institutional sources and footnote the NPS discrepancy.
claims.source: Library of Congress (citing Robert E. Weems Jr., 2020); Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (2019)

claims.claim: Douglass National Bank held national charter number 12227 and issued Series 1929 national bank notes.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; evidence is limited to artifact auction listings.
claims.evidence: Heritage Auctions and related numismatic listings identify charter no. 12227 and Series 1929 $5/$10 notes issued by Douglass National Bank of Chicago.
claims.notes: Auction listings establish the charter number's existence but are not a primary charter record; OCC charter records should be consulted for verification.
claims.source: Numismatic auction listings (Heritage Auctions)

claims.claim: Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan was founded in 1934 when 13 Black South Side leaders pooled $7,000, opening in a one-room office at 70 E. 47th Street in response to mortgage exclusion.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on founders, amount, or address.
claims.evidence: ProPublica (2021) reports the 13 founders, the $7,000 pool, and the 70 E. 47th Street one-room office.
claims.notes: A strong, journalism-sourced founding claim; the mortgage-exclusion motive is the reported rationale, not independently verified from founding documents.
claims.source: ProPublica, 'What's Gone Wrong at Chicago's Last Black-Owned Bank' (2021), https://www.propublica.org/article/whats-gone-wrong-at-chicagos-last-black-owned-bank

claims.claim: Illinois Service Federal's headquarters at 4619 S. Martin Luther King Drive was described in 1961 as a $1 million building with nearly $12 million in assets at the institution's 25-year mark.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; the 1961 Jet magazine caption was reached only indirectly and has not been independently verified.
claims.evidence: Secondary reference to a 1961 Jet magazine caption describing the $1 million building and ~$12 million in assets.
claims.notes: Do not treat the figures as verified balance-sheet data; the source chain is thin.
claims.source: Jet magazine (1961), via secondary citation

claims.claim: Groupe Nduom acquired Illinois Service Federal through a supervisory conversion in 2016 and renamed it GN Bank.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on the acquisition or renaming.
claims.evidence: ProPublica (2021) reports the 2016 acquisition and supervisory conversion; OCC records reference GN Bank as the institution's successor name.
claims.notes: The acquisition shifted ownership from local Black control to a Ghanaian-owned group — the ownership classification is addressed in C014.
claims.source: ProPublica (2021); Office of the Comptroller of the Currency enforcement records

claims.claim: GN Bank (the renamed Illinois Service Federal) remained in operation as of 2026; its current Black-owned/Black-controlled status is unresolved.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Third-party directories list it as active with FDIC certificate 29399, but official FDIC BankFind verification was not completed; Ghanaian ownership may qualify as African-owned but 'Black-owned' and local Black control require explicit evidence.
claims.evidence: Third-party banking directories report active status, FDIC certificate 29399, one Chicago office, and ~$60M in assets; no official ownership-classification evidence was located.
claims.notes: This is the brief's sharpest definitional test case for owned vs. controlled vs. serving — it must stay visible, not resolved by assertion.
claims.source: Third-party banking directories (2026); FDIC certificate reference 29399 (unverified via official BankFind)

claims.claim: On June 30, 2025, the OCC terminated GN Bank's September 18, 2020 consent order, stating the order's continued existence was no longer required for safety, soundness, and compliance.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: OCC enforcement action EA-AA-ENF-2025-39 (June 30, 2025) terminates the 2020 consent order with the quoted rationale.
claims.notes: This is a procedural termination, not a general 'safe and sound' certification — do not paraphrase it as such.
claims.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, enforcement action EA-AA-ENF-2025-39 (June 30, 2025), https://www.occ.gov/static/enforcement-actions/eaAA-ENF-2025-39.pdf

claims.claim: Independence Bank was founded in 1964 in Chicago's Chatham-Avalon area with $800,000 in initial capital; Alvin Boutte and George Johnson were among its founders.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; the detailed founder list rests on a single workspace source.
claims.evidence: CTL-DR-ECON-001 worker file W1-capital (notes.md) reports the 1964 founding, Chatham-Avalon location, $800,000 capitalization, and associates Boutte and Johnson with the founding.
claims.notes: Single-source within the sibling package — corroboration from press or charter records is needed before upgrading.
claims.source: CTL-DR-ECON-001 W1-capital worker notes (sibling package)

claims.claim: In 1988, Indecorp (Independence Bank's holding company) purchased the healthy white-owned Drexel National Bank — described as the first such purchase by a Black-controlled financial institution — and the combined company held approximately $279 million in assets.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; the 'first' characterization is Black Enterprise's.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise reports the 1988 Drexel acquisition, the 'first' characterization, and the ~$279 million combined-asset figure.
claims.notes: The asset figure is a single reported number; the episode is the strongest evidence for Black-controlled finance as corporate/municipal infrastructure.
claims.source: Black Enterprise, 'Great Moments in Black History No. 38: Indecorp's Big Deal — Buying a $100 Million White Bank', https://www.blackenterprise.com/great-moments-in-black-history-no-38-indecorps-big-deal-buying-a-100-million-white-bank/

claims.claim: ShoreBank acquired Indecorp in 1995, ending its Black-ownership status; ShoreBank itself later failed (2010).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise reports the 1995 ShoreBank acquisition and the loss of Black ownership; ShoreBank's 2010 failure is widely documented.
claims.notes: The proposed sale to Black-owned OmniBanc collapsed after rising interest rates reduced the value of Indecorp's bond-heavy portfolio (Black Enterprise) — a documented interest-rate-risk mechanism.
claims.source: Black Enterprise

claims.claim: Seaway Bank and Trust was established in 1965 to counter discriminatory South Side lending, opening at 8555 S. Cottage Grove; its later headquarters was at 645 E. 87th Street.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on founding year, motive, or addresses.
claims.evidence: Chicago Citizen 50th-anniversary coverage (2015) reports the 1965 founding, the anti-discrimination motive, and the Cottage Grove opening.
claims.notes: The founding motive is the institution's self-described rationale as reported in anniversary coverage.
claims.source: Chicago Citizen, 'Seaway Bank Marks 50th Anniversary' (2015), https://citizennewspapergroup.com/news/2015/jan/07/seaway-bank-marks-50th-anniversary/

claims.claim: Under Jacoby Dickens (chair 1983-2013), Seaway grew to over $500 million in assets with 11 branches, online banking, airport currency exchange, and acquisitions of failed institutions; he was succeeded by Veranda Dickens.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Individual operational 'firsts' (e.g., first Black-owned bank with online banking) need cautious grading.
claims.evidence: Secondary coverage reports the scale figures and Dickens's chairmanship; the 2013 Congressional Record tribute confirms his leadership and the bank's lending in depressed neighborhoods.
claims.notes: Scale figures are secondary-sourced; the civic-lending role is corroborated by the Congressional Record.
claims.source: Chicago Citizen (2015); Congressional Record, vol. 159 (2013), tribute to Jacoby Dickens, https://www.congress.gov/congressional-record/volume-159/issue-69/house-section/article/H2663-1

claims.claim: Seaway Bank and Trust failed on January 27, 2017; the State Bank of Texas assumed $307.1 million in deposits and purchased $309.0 million of $361.2 million in assets; the FDIC retained the remainder.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: FDIC primary press release (Jan. 27, 2017) gives the closure date, deposit assumption, asset purchase, and asset/deposit totals; the Illinois regulator's release confirms the 5 p.m. closure.
claims.notes: Primary regulator evidence — the brief's strongest failure-evidence case.
claims.source: FDIC press release (Jan. 27, 2017), https://archive.fdic.gov/view/fdic/6498/fdic_6498_DS1.pdf; Illinois Dept. of Financial and Professional Regulation release (Jan. 27, 2017)

claims.claim: In May 2017, Self-Help Federal Credit Union acquired $240 million of Seaway's deposits and nine branches from State Bank of Texas; State Bank of Texas retained the O'Hare branch and a ~$200 million loan portfolio.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located.
claims.evidence: Banking Exchange reporting quotes State Bank of Texas president Sushil Patel and Self-Help's Al Bass on the transaction structure and rationale.
claims.notes: Shows deposit continuity alongside ownership loss — a key 'endings' pattern for the brief.
claims.source: Banking Exchange, 'Minority-owned institutions dwindling' (2017)

claims.claim: Community Bank of Lawndale opened in June 1977 at 807 S. Homan Avenue with $2 million in starting capital, reportedly the first Black-owned bank on Chicago's West Side; Rev. Shelvin Jerome Hall founded it.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on date, address, capital, or founder.
claims.evidence: The HistoryMakers finding aid for Rev. Shelvin Jerome Hall identifies him as the bank's 1977 founder; secondary coverage corroborates the June 1977 opening, Homan Avenue address, $2 million capital, and West Side first.
claims.notes: Institutional-archive evidence for the founder; the 'first on the West Side' characterization is secondary.
claims.source: The HistoryMakers (Rev. Shelvin Jerome Hall finding aid); secondary coverage

claims.claim: Living Word Christian Center interests acquired Community Bank of Lawndale for $3 million in 2008, renamed it Covenant Bank, and drew investments from more than 3,000 church and community shareholders.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on the acquisition terms or investor count.
claims.evidence: Forest Park Review reports the $3 million acquisition, the 2008 date, the Covenant Bank renaming, and the 3,000+ shareholder base.
claims.notes: The church-led acquisition is the brief's strongest savings-mobilization episode in the modern era.
claims.source: Forest Park Review, 'Covenant Bank shut down by FDIC' (Feb. 16, 2013), https://www.forestparkreview.com/2013/02/16/covenant-bank-shut-down-by-fdic/

claims.claim: Covenant Bank was closed by Illinois regulators on February 15, 2013; Liberty Bank and Trust assumed all deposits; the bank had ~$58.4 million in assets and ~$54.2 million in deposits at year-end 2012.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None.
claims.evidence: FDIC failed-bank page and February 15, 2013 press release confirm the closure date, the Liberty Bank assumption, and the asset/deposit figures.
claims.notes: Distinguish insured depositors (transferred whole) from equity investors (wiped out).
claims.source: FDIC, Covenant Bank failure page and press release (Feb. 15, 2013), https://www.fdic.gov/resources/resolutions/bank-failures/failed-bank-list/covenant-il.html

claims.claim: Covenant Bank's failure involved bad real-estate rehabilitation loans during the downturn, a $3 million regulatory capital need, a $2.2 million loss through September 2012, and total loss for shareholders.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; multiple interacting causes are documented rather than a single cause.
claims.evidence: Forest Park Review reports the bad rehabilitation loans, the $3 million capital need, the $2.2 million nine-month loss, and the shareholder wipeout.
claims.notes: Keep multi-causal framing: real-estate concentration + undercapitalization + recession, not a single villain.
claims.source: Forest Park Review (Feb. 16, 2013)

claims.claim: African American minority depository institutions fell from 48 in 2001 to 23 at end-2018 (21 in 2019).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on the FDIC figures.
claims.evidence: FDIC (2019 speech) reports 48 in 2001 to 23 at end-2018; FDIC data show 21 in 2019.
claims.notes: National context for Chicago's contraction; do not infer individual-bank causes from the aggregate.
claims.source: FDIC, speech (Nov. 2019), https://fdic.gov/news/speeches/2019/spnov2019.html

claims.claim: Chicago had five African American-owned banks in 2001; after Seaway's failure only two remained.
claims.contradictory_evidence: The paper's 'black-owned' label may include institutions that were Black-serving rather than strictly Black-owned (see Urban Partnership discussion).
claims.evidence: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Toussaint-Comeau and Newberger (2017), Economic Perspectives, reports the 2001-to-post-Seaway contraction.
claims.notes: The definitional looseness in the source is itself evidence for the owned-vs-serving distinction the brief makes.
claims.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Economic Perspectives (2017), https://www.chicagofed.org/~/media/publications/economic-perspectives/2017/ep2017-4-pdf.pdf

claims.claim: FDIC research found minority depository institutions were about 2.5 times more likely to fail than non-MDI banks during the study period, while being smaller and serving economically stressed communities.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on the reported finding; it does not by itself establish causes for any individual Chicago failure.
claims.evidence: FDIC minority depository institution research reports the 2.5x failure-likelihood finding alongside the size and community-stress characteristics.
claims.notes: A structural finding, not a verdict on any single bank's management.
claims.source: FDIC MDI research

claims.claim: South Side Community Federal Credit Union (founded 2003, 5401 S. Wentworth Ave.) was described in 2018 as Chicago's only Black-owned community credit union; it reported over $5.5 million in low-interest loans and over 800 foreclosure preventions.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located.
claims.evidence: Chicago Reporter (2016) reports the $5.5 million in loans and 800 foreclosure preventions; 2018 coverage describes it as the city's only Black-owned community credit union.
claims.notes: Used as a bounded comparison showing 'Black finance' exceeded commercial banks; credit unions are member-owned, a different ownership model.
claims.source: Chicago Reporter, 'Banking on the Black Community' (2016), http://www.chicagoreporter.com/banking-on-the-black-community/

claims.claim: Urban Partnership Bank (ShoreBank's successor) is a Black-serving institution, not a Black-owned one — illustrating why 'owned,' 'controlled,' and 'serving' must be distinguished.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Some secondary sources loosely call it a Black-owned bank.
claims.evidence: The Chicago Fed (2017) paper treats Urban Partnership as a CDFI without MDI designation; ProPublica reporting distinguishes its ownership from its mission.
claims.notes: An analytic claim built from source comparison — the brief's definitional centerpiece.
claims.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (2017); ProPublica (2021)

grading_note: Grades: VERIFIED = primary/official record or converging institutional sources; SUPPORTED = multiple reputable secondary sources in agreement; PROVISIONAL = single or thin source; DISPUTED = conflicting sources (the Douglass 'first vs. second' conflict is documented inside C009 rather than as a standalone claim); UNRESOLVED = insufficient evidence. No claims below PROVISIONAL are used as evidence for the brief's findings.
notes: Ledger built 2026-09-28 from evidence assembled in-session. Claims are numbered C001-C031 and keyed to brief.md sections. Video sources illustrate but are never the sole evidence for a claim (see visuals.md).
